content: 1. For airborne cadmium concentrations less than or equal to 40 mg/m³, a half-mask respirator equipped with high-efficiency filters is recommended. Alternatively, a Type C demand-type supplied-air respirator with a half-mask facepiece can be used. 2. For concentrations of 40 mg/m³ or greater, or when the concentration is unknown, a full-facepiece respirator with high-efficiency filters is advised. Other options include a Type C demand-type supplied-air respirator with a full facepiece or a self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) with a full facepiece in demand mode. 3. For positive-pressure environments, a powered air-purifying respirator (PAPR) with high-efficiency filters or a Type C continuous-flow supplied-air respirator is recommended. 4. In cases requiring a combination of supplied-air and auxiliary self-contained air supply, a pressure-demand supplied-air respirator should be used. 5. The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 emphasizes the importance of standards to safeguard workers from increasing workplace hazards. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has developed a formal research system to establish valid criteria for effective standards based on health effects. 6. Recommended standards for occupational exposure to cadmium are derived from health effects data. The Secretary of Labor considers these recommendations alongside feasibility and implementation factors when developing regulatory standards. 7. Periodic reviews of criteria and standards ensure ongoing worker protection. Successive reports will be issued as research and epidemiological studies progress, and as sampling and analytical methods are refined. 8. Cadmium exposure is defined as exposure to concentrations exceeding the action level, which is half the time-weighted average environmental limit for cadmium. Lower concentrations do not require adherence to all sections except for specific provisions. 9. Medical evaluations for workers exposed to cadmium include chest X-rays, pulmonary function tests (FVC and FEV1), blood pressure measurements, blood analysis (e.g., BUN, complete blood count, liver enzymes), and urinalysis (e.g., protein quantification, specific gravity). Urine cadmium levels should also be determined. 10. Workers' ability to use positive or negative pressure respirators must be assessed. Urine protein determination methods must be quantitative and sensitive to low molecular weight proteins. 11. Periodic medical examinations should be offered annually, except for urine protein determinations, which should be conducted every four months. These examinations include interim work and medical histories, urinalysis, pulmonary function tests, and blood pressure measurements. Chest radiographs should be taken if deemed necessary by the physician. 12. Engineering controls should be implemented to maintain airborne cadmium concentrations at or below recommended limits. Respirators may only be used during installation/testing of controls, non-routine maintenance, single operations, or emergencies. 13. Employers must ensure proper respirator selection, fit, use, and maintenance to prevent overexposure to cadmium. Respirators must comply with American National Standards and be approved under 30 CFR 11. 14. Workers must be informed of cadmium hazards, symptoms of overexposure, emergency procedures, and precautions to minimize exposure. A continuing education program should ensure workers are knowledgeable about job hazards, maintenance procedures, and proper respirator use. 15. Work practices should include enclosing operations that generate cadmium exposure and providing local exhaust ventilation unless air sampling demonstrates compliance with limits. Effluent air must meet emission standards and should not be recirculated into the workplace. 16. Welding, brazing, or thermal cutting of cadmium-containing materials must use local exhaust ventilation to maintain cadmium concentrations within limits. For single operations without ventilation, respirators must be provided. 17. Emergency procedures must address substantial cadmium releases, including appropriate respirator use and fire protection measures for workers and firefighters. 18. Workers should wear designated work clothing, which must not be worn outside the workplace. Employers must provide proper laundry services and instruct launderers on avoiding cadmium dust inhalation. 19. Sanitation practices should prioritize vacuum or wet cleaning methods for cadmium-containing dust. Dry sweeping or blowing is prohibited. Prompt cleanup of spills and proper storage of cadmium materials are essential. 20. Facilities must protect food and consumption areas from cadmium contamination. Smoking and carrying uncovered tobacco products in cadmium work areas are prohibited. Adequate handwashing and shower facilities must be provided. 21. Industrial hygiene surveys must be conducted within 90 days of standard promulgation and repeated every three years or after process changes likely to increase airborne cadmium concentrations. Records of these surveys must be maintained. 22. Cadmium exposure has been linked to various health effects, including acute pulmonary edema, chronic proteinuria, renal dysfunction, olfactory damage, and potential carcinogenicity. Long-term exposure may also contribute to bone disease and anemia. 23. Epidemiological studies have identified occupational cadmium exposure as a risk factor for renal cancer and other health effects. However, dietary cadmium intake and smoking-related exposure require further investigation to establish definitive associations.
